extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (especially those doing worldbuilding and viewpoint-driven fiction)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for using character viewpoint and voice to deliver worldbuilding in fiction—how to show culture, rules, and setting through POV, dialogue, action, and contrasting perspectives. Focuses on craft choices (first vs third person, free indirect speech, unreliable viewpoint) and practical techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some voice in the text must speak definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: When you’re defining your world for the reader, some voice in the text must speak those definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worldbuilding should be conveyed through a character or narrative voice rather than as neutral, detached exposition. Let a voice—whether a POV character or an appropriately flavored narrator—present how the world works so the definitions feel embedded and purposeful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with how the character interacts physically and emotionally
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with the way the character interacts with the world, both physically and emotionally. Use the weight that things carry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show what objects and routines mean to that character (Jane Austen examples: a touch or removing a glove communicates social rules and emotional stakes). Use physical interactions to reveal cultural rules, not just visual description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use actions and dialogue to show assumptions and attitudes; avoid info-dumps
rubrics_metrics.description: Use actions and dialogue to show us assumptions and attitudes, how things work, without lengthy info dumps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed explanations in what characters do and say. For example, rather than explaining how magic flows, show a mechanic digging into a machine and naming parts as part of a POV-driven scene. Lean writing and in-scene discovery keep worldbuilding engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use two or more viewpoints with contrasting backgrounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Use two or more characters with different backgrounds or opinions, different viewpoints, to give the reader information about the thing, about the characters, and about the unreliable viewpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present the same object/event/ritual through contrasting perspectives so the reader learns about the world and the characters simultaneously and can detect bias or unreliability in perception (e.g., Children of Blood and Bone's three viewpoints; generational contrasts in post-apocalyptic fiction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Show the same person/event differently through differing observers
rubrics_metrics.description: One way to use viewpoint to intersect with worldbuilding is in the way characters describe other characters. The same character seen through the eyes of two different characters can be very different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrasting descriptions (tone, metaphor, judged traits) from different POVs to reveal social context and the observers' values. Example: one character sees someone as a blacksmith-forged type, another as a card-cheating thug—both signal toughness but through cultural lenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance character voice directing narrative vs narrator trustworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Think about how the character’s voice directs the narrative versus keeping the narrative safe and trustworthy. First person, the character runs everything. Third person, you need to balance. Some voice, some straight narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In first person, lean fully into the character's interpretations. In tight third, decide how much of the character's perceptions you let inflect 'objective' narration—too much unflagged voice can mislead readers into accepting a biased view as fact. Use clear signals (free indirect speech, stylistic cues) to mark subjective perception where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use viewpoint to create and manage unreliable or mistaken memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Viewpoints can be untrustworthy—characters misremember or conflate facts (e.g., Mary Robinette's example of a character conflating memories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately allow characters to be wrong or to misremember to add depth and ambiguity, but make it clear (through other perspectives, later revelation, or textual signals) that the viewpoint is unreliable so readers can interpret discrepancies intentionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey technical/process knowledge via POV action rather than exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: When explaining how things work—mechanical, magical, or procedural—show them through a character doing the work rather than long explanatory passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the POV character name parts, search, and discover problems within the scene (Howard's mechanic/Warjack example). This provides believable detail and keeps narrative momentum while educating the reader about the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make worldbuilding sentences do more than one thing at once
rubrics_metrics.description: Make your sentences, particularly your worldbuilding sentences, do more than one thing at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine physical description with character reaction/action (example: 'My character's heels clacked across the marble floor' both describes setting and character). Multi-tasking sentences deliver setting, characterization, tone, and plot economy simultaneously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cultural specifics—swear-phrases, jokes, gods—to signal belonging
rubrics_metrics.description: To make your worldbuilding richer, think about what people swear by, who makes what jokes, and how your character interacts with the environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinctive idioms, oaths, and humor signal cultural affiliation and social norms. NPCs using different invocations (swear by gods, taboo words) or different allowable jokes instantly mark cultural boundaries and character origins (ESO/NPCs example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use generational or experiential contrast as a worldbuilding tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Use differences in lived experience (e.g., people who remember life before an apocalypse vs those born after) to reveal societal change and values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presenting scenes from different generations or cohorts shows what was lost, what became normalized, and what each group values without exposition—contrasting reactions to the same environment reveals social history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish viewpoint-driven worldbuilding to avoid perceived inconsistencies
rubrics_metrics.description: If you rely on differing viewpoints or unreliable narrators, readers may flag apparent inconsistencies; you need to refine and polish so the intended perspective is clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On revision, check who is stating each fact and whether apparent contradictions are intentional. If a discrepancy is intentional (the speaker is wrong), ensure readers have markers to interpret it as such; otherwise, adjust wording to avoid accidental contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve perceptions for free indirect speech; treat third-person narration carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: With tight third, free indirect speech can carry perception; be deliberate about when you let character perception color the narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use free indirect style to slip into a character's perceptions without full first-person voice, but avoid unmarked slippage that leaves readers thinking the narrative voice is asserting facts the character merely believes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge problematic viewpoints without endorsing them
rubrics_metrics.description: You can present characters who hold objectionable perspectives (e.g., characters with a persistent male gaze) while showing how those behaviors are perceived in the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict such characters truthfully to their POV, but provide contextual signals (physicality, other characters' reactions, narration) that the text does not validate the viewpoint; this enables critique and complexity without endorsement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise: 'From within, from without'—write a scene twice from different perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Homework: Take a character who is alien to the culture/setting you’re writing, and describe things from their point of view. Now describe those same things from the point of view of a character native to the culture/setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This concrete exercise practices using outsider vs insider perceptions to expose cultural assumptions and highlight what details convey meaning to different observers. Use it to test how much world information each perspective naturally supplies.
